I think the issue is actually really simple. Microsoft, like all huge companies, needs a constant and very large revenue stream. The problem for them is two fold:

  1. They actually made a really great OS with Windows 7. Windows 8 uptake was certainly slow because the idea of a mobile interface on a desktop was pretty stupid, but it was also slow simply because people had 0 reason to upgrade. It's similarly how many people simply stopped upgrading after Windows XP for many years. It was a great OS for the time and it really took things like widespread 64 bit CPUs and the like to begin giving people a reason to upgrade. Without a major reason to upgrade, which Windows could not realistically offer, their next OS would face a similar fate as Windows 8.

  2. Desktop iteration rates have dramatically slowed. In the early 2000s if you bought a desktop it'd be pretty outdated 6 months later. Now if you buy a decent desktop it's going to be able to last you for years. If all you do is check your email, play some non intensive games, and browse the web - a desktop today would last you indefinitely.

The same is also true of things like Office. Now a days Libre Office is at least as functional as MS Office and it's completely free. And hardware manufacturers are also feeling the squeeze of things like diminishing iteration rates. Each time they squeeze Windows + various Microsoft software on their machines it substantially increases the final price. They've long since been noncompetitive against homemade machines and the excessive price of Microsoft's software isn't helping them any.

Microsoft is basically running out of ways to have a constant revenue stream. I think this is why they were trying to push the cloud so hard. It would have allowed them to constantly charge a monthly rate if caught on - it didn't. It's also why now they're trying to do things like offer Office as a service, and ultimately why they're turning their desktop software into an advertising and datamining system. Having your customers hate you is probably what they foresaw as an acceptable loss as a means to survival. I think many people just think of Microsoft as this money printing monster. We've had huge price inflation of most big public companies, especially in the tech sector, over the past decade due to quantitative easing as well as organic growth in the industry. All of this has completely passed up Microsoft. They reached their peak market valuation 18 years. Compare this to Apple who 18 years ago whose stock was worth about 1/100th of what it is today, or a random software company like Adobe who was worth 1/20th as much as it is today.
